title: Argument from Evidence: Plant Growth Materials

opener.title: Argument from Evidence: Plant Growth Materials
opener.question: Three different experiments, done in three different ways. Can they all point to the same answer about where a plant's mass comes from?
opener.alt: An opening film that starts on the green chloroplasts inside leaf cells and zooms out to a lettuce leaf, a lettuce lifted out of water with bare roots, a farm that grows lettuce in pipes of water, farm fields seen from space, and finally the whole Earth.

frames.label: Leaf cells, under a microscope
frames.scale: less than half a millimeter across
frames.line: These green dots are chloroplasts, packed inside the cells of a leaf. This is where a plant builds its food.

frames.label: A lettuce leaf
frames.line: Zoom out. A lettuce leaf, made of millions of those cells.

frames.label: Lettuce grown in water, with no soil
frames.line: This lettuce is being lifted out of its tray. Look at its long white roots. There is no soil anywhere.

frames.label: A farm that grows lettuce in pipes of water
frames.line: Some farms grow lettuce like this, in rows of pipes filled with water.

frames.label: Farm fields in Kansas, seen from a satellite
frames.line: Farther out. Farm fields, seen from space. Every green circle is a crop, growing bigger every day.

frames.label: Planet Earth
frames.line: And all of it on one planet, wrapped in a thin layer of air.

k-warmup.text: Today you are the judge. Look at the lettuce in this photo. It grew to full size. Slide to show how many cups of soil you think it used up as it grew. Then write one reason. Your prediction is saved, and you'll find out the real answer in Part 3.

k-words.text: These six words are the tools of a scientific argument. Tap a word sticker. You'll hear it, and the card shows what it means. Try to tap all six.

k-part1.text: This is a real page from seventeen seventy-two, by Joseph Priestley. Tap a yellow line to hear it in plain English. Then sort his sentences. Which one is his claim? Which ones are evidence? Then look for the reasoning. Priestley left that part out, so you'll pick it.

k-part2.text: Now run Priestley's jars yourself. Before each step, make a prediction. A candle burns until it goes out. Then the mint goes in. Wait the days, and test both jars with a lit candle.

k-part3.text: Here comes the other side. Press play on each quote. Then tap the evidence card that answers it best. One card is true, but it doesn't answer any of them.

k-part4.text: Two more witnesses. First, predict what the carbon dioxide number will do in a sealed jar. Then run the jar in the light, and switch the light off. Watch the meter. After that, predict which tray of seedlings gains more mass.

k-wow.text: Priestley's page never says whether his jars sat in the light. Later, his test did not always work, and he could not tell why. The missing piece was light. Careful scientists can still leave something out. That's why the chain keeps going.

k-assign.text: Now add your page to the chain. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, explain how Priestley's page and van Helmont's page agree, and what you would ask Priestley. Then use the planner to build your C-E-R.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to hear it and see what it means.

words.def: A sentence that answers the question. It says what you think is true.
Data or observations that support a claim. Anyone should be able to check it.
The explanation of why your evidence proves your claim. It connects the dots.
An idea many people believe that the evidence does not support.
A gas in the air. Plants take it in through their leaves and use it to build sugar.
How plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar for growing.

source.title: Joseph Priestley's own words
source.alt: A printed page from 1772 in old-style type, where the letter s often looks like an f. It describes putting a sprig of mint into air where a candle had burned out.
source.intro: Joseph Priestley was an English scientist. He read this report to the Royal Society, a group of scientists in London, in 1772. Old printers often used a long s that looks like an f, so “ſprig” means sprig.
job: Tap each yellow line to hear it in plain English.
Then sort his sentences in the game below the page.

lines.en: I found that candles burn very well in air where plants have grown for a long time. So I wondered if plants could also fix air that a burning candle had spoiled.
So on August seventeenth, seventeen seventy-one, I put a sprig of mint into air in which a wax candle had burned out.
On the twenty-seventh of the same month, another candle burned perfectly well in it.
I did this eight or ten times in the rest of the summer, and it worked every time.

Many times I split the spoiled air into two jars. I put the plant in one and left the other the same way, but with no plant. A candle always burned in the jar with the plant, and never in the other one.
When the plant was healthy, five or six days were usually enough to fix the air. Without a plant, I kept this air for many months, and it did not change at all.
Experiments in seventeen seventy-two strongly confirmed my conclusion: growing plants fix air in which candles have burned out.

source.credit: Source: Joseph Priestley, “Observations on Different Kinds of Air,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, volume 62 (1772), page 168. Scan from the Internet Archive (public domain). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

sort.title: Sort Priestley's sentences
sort.intro: A scientific argument has a claim, evidence, and reasoning. Here are four of Priestley's sentences, in plain English.
job: Tap a sentence, then tap Claim or Evidence. You can also drag it.
Then pick the reasoning Priestley left out.

bins.label: Evidence
bins.sub: What he saw that anyone could check

cards.t: On August 27, another candle burned perfectly well in the mint's jar.
cards.yes: Yes. That is evidence. Anyone could light a candle and check.

cards.t: I put the plant in one jar and no plant in the other. A candle always burned in the jar with the plant, and never in the other one.
cards.yes: Yes. That is evidence, and a careful test: two jars that are the same except for the plant.

cards.t: Growing plants fix air in which candles have burned out.
cards.yes: Yes. That is his claim: it says what he thinks is true.

cards.t: Without a plant, I kept this air for many months, and it did not change at all.
cards.yes: Yes. That is evidence too. It shows the air does not fix itself.

no.claim: A claim says what is true in general. This sentence tells what he saw happen, so it is something anyone could check.
no.evidence: This sentence doesn't describe one thing he saw. It says what is true about all growing plants.

sort.sortedNote: All four are sorted: one claim and three pieces of evidence. But where is the reasoning?

reason.q: Priestley never wrote down his reasoning. Which sentence connects his evidence to his claim?

opts.t: The only difference between the two jars was the plant, so the plant must be what fixed the air.

opts.hint: That's true, but it doesn't explain why one jar was fixed and the other wasn't.

opts.t: Mint smells fresh, so it makes air better.
opts.hint: His jars didn't test smell. Look for the sentence that uses what was different between the two jars.

reason.win: Yes. Reasoning explains WHY the evidence proves the claim. Only the plant was different, so the plant made the difference.

jars.title: Run Priestley's jars
jars.why: Why this matters: van Helmont weighed a tree. Priestley did something totally different with a candle and a sprig of mint. If two different methods point to the same answer, the argument gets much stronger.
job: Before each step, make a prediction.
Let the candle burn out, then put the mint in Jar A.
Wait the days, then test both jars with a lit candle.

plate.alt: An old engraving of glass jars standing upside down in a tub of water. A sprig of a plant stands inside the tall jar on the right.
plate.caption: Priestley's own drawing of his equipment, from his book about kinds of air (1774). Find the sprig of a plant in the tall jar on the right.

text: Priestley set a lit wax candle under a glass jar standing in water. The candle burned until it went out on its own.
The candle used up something in the air. Priestley split this spoiled air into two jars, Jar A and Jar B.
Now Priestley slides a sprig of mint into Jar A. Jar B stays the same, with no plant.
The mint is in Jar A. Jar B has the same spoiled air, but no plant.
Now wait. Priestley waited ten days.
Ten days have passed. Time to test the air.

relight.q: If he lowers a new lit candle into this air now, what will happen?
relight.miss: It goes out right away. The air is still spoiled.

test.q: After ten days, in which jar will a lit candle burn?
test.miss: Only Jar A. The mint made the difference.

jars.quote: On the 27th of the same month, another candle burned perfectly well in it.
jars.win: The candle burns in Jar A but goes out in Jar B. The only difference was the mint, so the mint changed the air. Two witnesses now agree: van Helmont's willow and Priestley's mint both point to the air.

otherside.title: Hear the other side
otherside.why: Here are three things people really say. Saying “you're wrong” won't change a mind. Evidence will.
job: Tap the evidence card that answers it best.

quotes.t: Plants eat soil. That's why their roots grow down into the dirt.
quotes.yes: Lettuce grows full size with its roots in water and no soil at all. Roots take in water, not soil.

quotes.t: A tree gets its wood from the soil. Where else could all that wood come from?
quotes.yes: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds, but the soil lost only about 2 ounces. The wood did not come from the soil.

quotes.t: Farmers add fertilizer, so fertilizer must be the plant's food.
quotes.yes: Fertilizer adds a few nutrients, like vitamins for a plant. The plant builds its body from carbon dioxide and water.

cards.alt: Lettuce lifted out of water, with long bare roots.
cards.title: Lettuce in water
cards.text: Grows full size with its roots in water. No soil at all.

cards.title: Van Helmont's willow
cards.text: Gained about 164 pounds. The soil lost about 2 ounces.

cards.title: What fertilizer is
cards.text: A few nutrients a plant needs in tiny amounts, like vitamins.

cards.title: Plants need light
cards.text: Plants kept in the dark stop gaining mass.
cards.hint: That's true evidence, but it doesn't answer any of these three quotes. Try another card.

otherside.wrong: That card is true, but it answers a different quote. Read this quote again and look for the card that matches it.

cupsReveal.text: The lettuce used up no soil at all, because it never grew in soil. Its whole body was built from water, carbon dioxide from the air, and a few nutrients in the water.

otherside.credit: Photos: Preston Keres, USDA (public domain); young willow, Юрий Д.К., Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

meter.intro: Witness A was van Helmont's willow. Now test Witness C, a plant sealed in a jar with a carbon dioxide sensor, and Witness B, seedlings kept in a dark box.

jar.title: Witness C: the sealed jar
job: Predict what the carbon dioxide number will do.
Run the jar with the light on for at least 2 hours.
Then switch the light off and run it for at least 1 and a half hours.

predict.q: A plant is sealed in a clear jar under a bright lamp. What will happen to the carbon dioxide in the jar?

jar.note: This is a model. Its numbers follow how real sealed-jar tests with carbon dioxide sensors behave: in light, a plant pulls the carbon dioxide in a jar far down, and in the dark the number slowly rises again.
jar.q: What happened when the light was off?

opts.t: The carbon dioxide kept going down
opts.hint: Look at the shaded part of the graph, where the light was off. Which way does the line go there?

opts.t: It stopped going down and slowly crept back up
It dropped all the way to zero
opts.hint: Read the meter during the dark part. Did it ever reach zero?

jar.win: In the dark, the plant can't use carbon dioxide to build sugar, so the number stops falling. It even creeps up, because plants breathe out a little carbon dioxide all the time, like you do. Light is the energy that powers the building.

trays.title: Witness B: the dark box
trays.intro: Two trays of bean seedlings got the same soil and the same water. One tray sat in sunlight. The other sat in a dark box for two weeks.

predict.q: Which tray will gain more mass?
opts: The tray in the dark box

trays.alt: Pale yellow-white bluebell leaves that grew under a cover, next to normal green leaves.
trays.caption: Real plants show the same thing. These pale leaves grew under a cover with no light. The green ones next to them grew in light.
trays.credit: Photo: Chiswick Chap, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
trays.result: The sunny plants were green and sturdy. The dark plants were pale and thin, and they stopped gaining mass, even with plenty of water.
trays.lightNote: Light has no mass, so it can't be what a plant is made of. Light is the energy a leaf uses to build sugar out of carbon dioxide and water. No light, no building.

rows: Witness C: carbon dioxide in the sealed jar
Witness B: which tray gained more mass
It went down in the light

twist.quote: Experiments made in the year 1772 abundantly confirmed my conclusion.
twist.line: But Priestley's page never says whether his jars sat in the light. Later his test did not always work, and he couldn't tell why. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz found the missing piece: a plant fixes the air only when light shines on it.
twist.chain: 📓 That is next week's page in the Notebook Chain: Ingenhousz and his leaves in the sunlight.

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: The willow gained about 164 pounds, but the soil lost only about 2 ounces.
Priestley's mint fixed air that a candle had spoiled, and a candle burned in it again.
In a sealed jar in the light, a plant pulled the carbon dioxide way down.
Plants kept in the dark stopped gaining mass, even with water.
Lettuce grows full size with its roots in water and no soil.
Light is energy, not matter, so it adds no mass.

Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.

cabinet.title: The biggest seed in the world
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a coco de mer seed: a large, dark brown seed with two rounded halves joined in the middle.
cabinet.text: This is a real seed from the Smithsonian. It comes from the coco de mer, a palm that grows wild on just two small islands in the Seychelles, in the Indian Ocean. It is the largest seed of any plant. One seed can weigh about 40 pounds. But the palm it grows into can stand about 100 feet tall and weigh far more than its seed. So even the biggest seed on Earth can't hold a whole tree. The rest is built from carbon dioxide and water.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Lodoicea maldivica (coco de mer) seed, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Botany. CC0.

footage.title: The whole planet's plants, from space
footage.intro: A NASA satellite called SeaWiFS measured the color of the land and the ocean for years. Green means plants. This clip shows five years of seasons in 20 seconds. In the ocean, the bright colors are tiny floating plants called phytoplankton.
look: Watch the land in the north turn dark green each summer and fade each winter.
Look for bright blooms in the ocean in spring.
Every bit of that green is building itself out of carbon dioxide and water.
footage.credit: Video: “Five Spheres: Biosphere,” NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio, SeaWiFS data, October 2001 to September 2006 (public domain). Slowed slightly for this lesson.

data.title: Two places, two witnesses
data.intro: Scientists measure the carbon dioxide in the air every hour at Utqiaġvik, a town at the top of Alaska, and at the South Pole. Here are the monthly averages for five years.
job: Drag across the graph to read both places in the same month.
Compare how much each line zigzags in one year.
data.ask: Which place has the bigger zigzag every year?

opts.hint: Look at the red line. Does it rise and fall much in a year? Now look at the blue one.

data.win: Yes. Alaska sits near the huge forests and fields of the north. Every summer they pull carbon dioxide out of the air, and every winter it comes back. The South Pole is ice, far from almost all plants, so its line barely wiggles. Two places, one answer: plants take carbon dioxide out of the air.
data.alt: A line graph of carbon dioxide from 2021 to 2025. The Alaska line zigzags up and down about 18 parts per million every year. The South Pole line is almost smooth.
data.credit: Data: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, in-situ monthly carbon dioxide at Utqiaġvik (Barrow), Alaska, and the South Pole, January 2021 to December 2025 (public data, downloaded November 8, 2026).
